parts.title: Hiring a wedding photographer
parts.context: A man phones a photographer about his wedding.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a photographer about his wedding. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Good morning, Sandra Reid Photography.

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: Hello. I'm getting married in the summer, and I'd like to ask about your wedding photography. The ceremony and the party are both in a barn.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: That sounds lovely. Let me take a few details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The wedding is in a barn, so 'barn' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: Ryan Pemberton. That's P-E-M-B-E-R-T-O-N.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Thank you, Mr Pemberton. And what's the date of the wedding?

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: The twenty-first of June.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: That's a Saturday, and I'm free. How many guests will there be?

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: We said eighty at first, but we've cut the list, so it will be sixty.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: What time does the ceremony start?

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: At two o'clock in the afternoon. The party follows, with dinner and dancing.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: How long would you like me to stay? Some couples want me until midnight, but that costs extra.

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: No, nine in the evening will be enough. We're not very good at staying up late.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Then I'd suggest our standard package. It covers eight hours of photography, which is enough from the preparations in the morning until the first dance.

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: And how much is that?

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Eighty pounds an hour, so it's a fixed price for the day. We also offer an album, with forty pages. Extra copies for your parents cost thirty pounds each.

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: That's a nice idea. When will we get the photographs?

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Within four weeks. I choose the best five hundred or so and edit them, and I'll send you the first few pictures after a week, so that you can share them.

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: How are they delivered?

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: In an online gallery, which only you and your guests can see. You can download any picture you like, and the gallery stays open for a year.

script.speaker: ryan
script.text: That sounds ideal. Can we meet before the wedding?

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Of course. Come to my studio any weekday, and we'll talk about the pictures you'd like.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A country house for weddings
parts.context: An estate manager shows a couple round a country house.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear an estate manager showing a couple round a country house that can be hired for weddings. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: Welcome to Ashcombe House. I'm Gerald Ellison, the estate manager, and I'll show you around today. First, some background. The house was built in seventeen eighty for a wealthy wool merchant. Many people assume it's older, because of the style, but it was built to look like a much earlier building.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: The Great Hall is the largest room, and it seats a hundred and twenty guests at round tables. We can fit more with long tables, but then it feels crowded, and we don't recommend it.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: The price includes tables, chairs and linen. It doesn't include flowers or music, which you arrange yourselves, and we can suggest local people if you need help.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: If it rains, don't worry. All the outdoor events can be moved into the Barn, which is large and well heated, and many couples now choose it even when the weather is fine.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: Our diary fills up fast. I'd advise booking a year ahead for a summer wedding, although we sometimes have cancellations, so it's always worth asking.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: Now let me tell you which room is used for each part of the day. The ceremony takes place in the Orangery, which is a glass building with a view of the lake. It's the most popular place for the vows.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: Afterwards, the drinks reception is held on the Terrace, if the weather allows, with a view over the gardens, and the guests can walk around while the photographs are taken.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: The wedding dinner is in the Great Hall, as I said, and then the dancing happens in the Barn, so that the music won't disturb anyone else in the house.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: Many couples have children among their guests, so we also offer the Library as a children's room. We provide games and a film, and a member of staff stays with the children, so that the parents can relax.

script.speaker: agent
script.text: The Garden Room and the Cellar are also available, but they're normally used for meetings and for small private dinners. Shall we go and see the Orangery?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A study of politeness in emails
parts.context: Two linguistics students discuss the results of their study.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two linguistics students, Leah and Idris, discussing their study of politeness in emails. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: Idris, I've finished coding the emails for our politeness study. Shall I tell you what I found?

script.speaker: idris
script.text: Please. Our hypothesis was that students use more formal language when they ask for something.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: That was partly right. What made the biggest difference to how polite an email seemed was the greeting. Emails that began with 'Hi' were rated as much less polite than those beginning 'Dear Dr Evans'.

script.speaker: idris
script.text: And the exclamation marks?

script.speaker: leah
script.text: They had an effect too. The lecturers thought they sounded over-friendly, even a bit rude. The length of the email and the font didn't matter at all, and nobody commented on the time it was sent.

script.speaker: idris
script.text: How many emails did we analyse?

script.speaker: leah
script.text: Two hundred, from forty students, so five each.

script.speaker: idris
script.text: Were the students from different countries?

script.speaker: leah
script.text: Yes, about half were international students. Surprisingly, they were more formal than the home students.

script.speaker: idris
script.text: And did the lecturers' replies match the level of formality?

script.speaker: leah
script.text: Most did, but a few were noticeably more formal than the students, which made the students look casual.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: What will the discussion say about gender?

script.speaker: idris
script.text: That there was no significant difference between men and women, which contradicts what some earlier studies found.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: And the limitations?

script.speaker: idris
script.text: The main one is that we only looked at emails to lecturers, so we can't say anything about emails to friends or employers.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: How shall we present the data?

script.speaker: idris
script.text: A table of the ten most common greetings, with the average politeness score for each.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: I'll write the conclusion. I want to recommend that universities give students some guidance.

script.speaker: idris
script.text: That's sensible. A short guide with sample emails, perhaps.

script.speaker: leah
script.text: Our deadline is the fourteenth. If we finish drafting by Friday, we'll have a week to edit.

script.speaker: idris
script.text: Then let's aim for Friday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.explanation: The greeting (A) and exclamation marks (C) mattered. Length, font and time did not.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of timekeeping
parts.context: A lecture on how clocks developed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of timekeeping. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we'll look at how people have measured time, from the earliest devices to the clocks in our pockets.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The oldest instrument is the sundial, which was used in ancient Egypt. It has two obvious weaknesses: it does not work at night, and it does not work when the sky is cloudy. So people also developed water clocks, which measured time by the steady flow of water from one container into another.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. They were built mainly for monasteries, to call monks to prayer at the right hours. Early clocks had no face and no hands. They simply struck a bell, and the word clock itself comes from a word for bell.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Accuracy remained poor until sixteen fifty-six, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens built a clock regulated by a pendulum. It reduced the error from about fifteen minutes a day to about fifteen seconds a day.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: At sea, knowing the time was a matter of life and death, because sailors needed it to find their longitude. In the eighteenth century, John Harrison built a marine chronometer that kept accurate time despite the motion of a ship, and it solved the problem.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the twentieth century, the quartz clock used the vibrations of a crystal, which are extremely regular, and it made accurate watches cheap. Then came the atomic clock, which counts the vibrations of atoms, and the best of them lose less than a second in millions of years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One more development was social. With the spread of railways, every town used its own local time, which caused chaos with timetables, so countries introduced standard time zones. Today, most people simply check the time on their phones, which synchronise themselves with atomic clocks. Next week we'll look at calendars.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
